answer:
HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded answer): Yes — the SES→degree-completion relationship is affected by racial lines. Higher SES is associated with higher odds of BA-degree completion for every racial group, but the positive SES effect is substantially steeper for Black (and, directionally, Hispanic) respondents than for White respondents. This is a moderation (interaction) effect layered on top of a large racial gap in base completion rates (White 3.54% vs Hispanic 1.44% vs Black 1.33%).

KEY STATISTICS — Primary unadjusted logistic model  deg ~ SES_z × race (White reference), n=8,773, 236 completions:
- SES main effect (=White slope): +0.161 (OR 1.17 per +1 SD, p=0.031)
- SES×Black: +0.565 (95% CI 0.194–0.935 on log-odds; OR 1.76; p=0.0028)
- SES×Hispanic: +0.338 (95% CI −0.081–0.757; p=0.114, not significant alone)
- Marginal SES slope by race: White +0.161 (OR 1.17) < Hispanic +0.499 (OR 1.65) < Black +0.726 (OR 2.07)
- JOINT SES×race interaction: Wald χ²(2)=10.33, p=0.0057; LR χ²(2)=9.57, p=0.0083 → statistically significant.

ROBUSTNESS:
- L2-regularized logistic (5-fold-CV α=2.42): SES×Black +0.493, SES×Hispanic +0.295 — same direction and similar magnitude as the MLE.
- Sensitivity model adding academic controls (ASVAB composite, percentile-in-class): the interaction remains significant (Wald p=0.018, LR p=0.022; SES×Black +0.559 p=0.006), though the SES main effect attenuates/flips negative (−0.270) once academic performance is controlled — exactly the attenuation we kept out of the primary answer.

POWER / HONESTY: Only 28 Black and 19 Hispanic completions. The significant joint interaction is driven mainly by the Black–White contrast; the Hispanic contrast is directionally consistent (steeper slope than White) but individually non-significant under this sample size. Bivariate point-biserial corr(SES,degree) by race (Black 0.092 > Hispanic 0.069 > White 0.030) corroborates the same ordering.

payload.hypothesis: The relation between socioeconomic status and chances of BA-degree completion is affected by racial lines: the positive SES effect is significantly stronger (steeper slope) for Black respondents than for White respondents, and directionally so for Hispanic respondents, on top of a large racial gap in base completion rates (White ~3.5% vs Black/Hispanic ~1.3-1.4%).
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (n=8,773; 0 missing in all 8 fields). Treated BA DEGREE COMPLETED as a binary outcome (236/8,773 = 2.69%) and SES as a z-standardized continuous predictor; race as categorical with White reference. PRIMARY: unadjusted logistic model deg ~ SES_z * race, testing the two SES x race interaction terms jointly (2-df Wald and likelihood-ratio). Cross-checked with a 5-fold-CV-tuned L2-regularized logistic fit. SENSITIVITY: same interaction model + ASVAB composite and percentile-in-class as academic controls (kept separate so control-attenuation does not muddy the core answer). Also ran stratified per-race bivariate models. Estimator note: Firth's penalized likelihood (intended for rare events) was implemented and attempted, but its log-cos(eta/2) penalty is only defined for |eta|<pi, which a 2.7% base rate violates (intercept ~ -3.6), making the penalized likelihood degenerate; the plain maximum-likelihood logistic estimate (valid: SES is continuous, so no complete separation) was therefore used as primary, with L2-CV as the robustness fallback.
